Richard Davies
rich'ard da'vis
n. (Richard Davies, c. 1501–1581, Marian exile and Bishop of St Davids, co-translator of the Welsh New Testament)
Germanic Ricohard, strong in rule; Welsh Davies, son of David.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Richard Davies went into exile at Frankfurt under Mary, returned at Elizabeth's accession, and was made Bishop of St Davids, where he gave himself to the Welsh Scriptures. He translated part of the 1567 New Testament, pressed the project through, and wrote the long Welsh preface to it, addressed to his countrymen, which argued that the Britons had received a pure apostolic Christianity long before Augustine of Canterbury came, that Rome had afterwards imposed on them, and that the Reformation was therefore a restoration of what the Welsh had once had. The dictionary quotes that argument with care. Its historical reconstruction is partly legend, and the dictionary does not pretend otherwise; but its theological instinct is exactly right, and it is the instinct of the whole Reformation: what is being recovered is older than what is being removed. Davies told the Welsh that Protestantism was not an English novelty imposed upon them, and on the substance he was correct.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines preface as an introduction to a discourse or book, and primitive as original, of the earliest age.

expand to see more

PREF'ACE, n. Something spoken as introductory to a discourse, or written as introductory to a book.

PRIM'ITIVE, a. Pertaining to the beginning or origin; original; first; as the primitive church.

RESTORA'TION, n. The act of replacing in a former state; renewal; revival; re-establishment.

BISH'OP, n. An overseer; a spiritual superintendent, ruler or director.

Key Scripture

Jer 6:16 — "Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein."

Jud 1:3 — "Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

Act 17:11 — "These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so."

Gal 1:9 — "As we said before, so say I now again, If any man preach any other gospel unto you than that ye have received, let him be accursed."

Modern Corruption

His Welsh preface of 1567 told his countrymen the Reformation restored what Britain had held before Rome came.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the charge, as old as the Reformation and still in use, that Protestantism is a sixteenth-century invention and therefore an innovation. Davies answered it on two levels. His historical level — an ancient British church independent of Rome — is embroidered. His doctrinal level is sound and sufficient on its own: the faith the Reformers preached is the faith delivered once to the saints, and the additions are what came later.

The principle to recover is that the old way is the test and the new teaching bears the burden of proof. “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16). The faith was delivered once: “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). It is tested against Scripture and not against pedigree — “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) — and any later gospel stands condemned: “If any man preach any other gospel unto you than that ye have received, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:9).

Hebrew nethibah (H5410), a path, a way; Greek hapax (G530), once, once for all.

Usage

"“ask for the old paths, where is the good way” (Jer 6:16) — the preface to the Welsh New Testament."

"“the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) — Reformation as restoration, not novelty."

"“let him be accursed” (Gal 1:9) — a Marian exile who came home to St Davids."
